sources.title: Violeta Parra (Q230499), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-31): label 'Violeta Parra', description 'Chilean musician and folklorist', born 4 October 1917, died 5 February 1967, Korean label present, image 'Parra01f.PNG'. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Jnan Ananda Blau and the Editors of Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Violeta Parra', Britannica (published 1 February 2026), read in full. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: a Chilean composer, folk singer and social activist best known as one of the founders of the Nueva Cancion movement, who also painted, wrote poetry, sculpted and wove arpilleras; 'Gracias a la vida' as her best-known song; her 1952 journey through Chile to record folk music, encouraged by her brother, as the inspiration for the movement; the 1954 Caupolican prize, the trip to Poland, the Soviet Union and Europe and the stay in Paris. Encyclopedia entry; its political and personal passages are not scored.

Memoria Chilena (Biblioteca Nacional de Chile), 'Violeta Parra (1917-1967)', main biographical article and chronology, read in full (about 1,500 words of Spanish): radio artist, composer and folk collector, visual artist and poet; a reference for Chilean popular music; much of the Chilean musical movement from the 1950s starting from her and her family; the chronology of her first records (1949), Radio Chilena programmes (1953), the Caupolican prize (1955), the stay in Paris, the 1958 folk-art museum, the 1964 Paris exhibition, the 1965 tent and the last album. National library heritage portal; admiring in tone, and it also records personal and health material that is not used.

Memoria Chilena, 'Compositora y recopiladora' (Violeta Parra minisite), read in full (about 450 words): her professional start singing popular genres with her sister, then the 'applied and meticulous' research and composing of the 1950s, travelling the central valley to meet popular singers such as Rosa Lorca and Isaias Angulo (who taught her the guitarron), the recovery of rural song, the 1958 founding of the National Museum of Folk Art in Concepcion under the University of Concepcion, and academic appreciation of her experiments with melody, harmony and instrumental technique. National library heritage portal; evaluative sentences are not attributed to named scholars.

Memoria Chilena, 'Artista plastica' (Violeta Parra minisite), read in full (about 400 words): arpilleras, clay and wire work, the 1959 first arts fair on the Mapocho, the later work made in Geneva, the 18 April to 11 May 1964 exhibition at the Pavillon de Marsan of the Museum of Decorative Arts of the Louvre obtained 'after a great effort of management', and the later view of her work as among the most authentic and innovative of Chilean popular art. National library heritage portal; one author, not footnoted.

Memoria Chilena, 'Espacios' (Violeta Parra minisite), read in full (about 400 words): the trains, circuses and restaurants of her early performing, the Pena de los Parra opened in 1965 on her children's initiative (where she was not the organiser), and her tent in La Reina, opened on 17 December 1965 to become a centre of folk activity, which it says began well attended and over time was a failure. The source's link between that failure and her death is an interpretation and is not used. National library portal, the counter-voice on the tent project.

Memoria Chilena, 'Industria musical' (Violeta Parra minisite), read in full (about 650 words): her 1949 first single, her own radio programme 'Canta Violeta Parra' (January to September 1954, recorded largely at folk locations), the 1955 Caupolican prize as folklorist of the year, the Odeon LPs in the 'El folclore de Chile' series, her television appearances and her last album 'Ultimas composiciones' (released January 1967) with 'Gracias a la vida'. National library portal; detailed dates and titles.

Lorna Dillon (ed.), 'Violeta Parra: Life and Work' (Tamesis, 2017), record and abstract in the University of Kent repository, read in full (abstract only; the book was not opened): she is best known for her contribution to the Latin American New Song movement and for her visual art exhibited at the Louvre's Museum of Decorative Arts in 1964; the volume treats her music, paintings, sculptures, arpilleras and poetry, the Louvre exhibition and the Carpa de la Reina, with essays by Patricio Manns, Leonidas Morales and Ericka Verba among others. Scholarly edited volume known only through its abstract.

University of North Carolina Press, 'Thanks to Life: A Biography of Violeta Parra' by Ericka Kim Verba (2025), publisher's description and excerpted reviews, read in full (the book was not opened): a self-taught visual artist who exhibited at the Louvre's Museum of Decorative Arts, a biography based on decades of research that covers her creative, political and personal life 'flaws and all', and Booklist's remark that she studied Chilean folklore to excavate the past. Publisher and review excerpts, so promotional; the political framing is not scored.

Eloise Ptito, 'Gracias a la vida: Violeta Parra's Textiles', Selvedge magazine, 14 January 2021, read in full (about 350 words): her large and confrontational arpilleras, which differ from the traditional small format, her description of them as 'songs that are painted', the blend of nineteenth-century popular graphics with a modern palette, the April 1964 Louvre exhibition of arpilleras, oil paintings and wire sculptures, and the 1965 Maspero book of her popular poetry. Short textile-magazine article, mostly secondary.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_vp_eb, src_vp_mc_bio, src_vp_mc_art, src_vp_kent, src_vp_selvedge | 1930s-1966 | encyclopedia + national library + scholarly abstract + magazine] Four independent descriptions agree that besides composing and singing she wrote poetry (a 1965 Maspero book of popular poetry), made arpilleras, oil paintings, wire sculptures and clay figures, and exhibited the visual work at the Louvre's Museum of Decorative Arts in 1964. The breadth is documented consistently; how deeply she mastered each medium is judged less consistently. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed as a top-risk row and kept, since the breadth is documented by four independent sources.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_vp_eb, src_vp_mc_comp, src_vp_mc_art, src_vp_selvedge | 1952-1966 | encyclopedia + national library + magazine] Britannica says her work synthesised Chilean folk traditions with concern for social conditions, Memoria Chilena says academics value her experiments with melody, harmony, instrumental technique and voice, and the magazine describes arpilleras of unusual scale that blend nineteenth-century popular graphics with a modern palette. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed as a top-risk row; lowered from 74 / 0.60 to 70 / 0.54 because the originality judgements come from a national heritage portal and publisher or magazine praise, with no critical musicological analysis read and none naming a scholar.

curiosity.rationale: [src_vp_eb, src_vp_mc_comp, src_vp_mc_industria | 1952-1959 | encyclopedia + national library] From 1952 she travelled through Chile to record folk music, met popular singers such as Rosa Lorca and Isaias Angulo and learned the guitarron from the latter, and her radio programme was recorded largely at folk locations. The sources describe her research as applied and meticulous and as the source of her later composing; the evidence is a documented pattern of fieldwork, but the description of its quality is the portal's own.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_vp_mc_comp, src_vp_mc_art, src_vp_mc_espacios, src_vp_kent | 1958-1965 | national library + scholarly abstract] She founded the National Museum of Folk Art in Concepcion in January 1958, obtained the 1964 Louvre exhibition after a great effort of management, and opened her own tent in La Reina in December 1965 as a folk centre, which the portal says did not succeed. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed as a top-risk row; lowered from 72 / 0.58 to 68 / 0.52 because the 'great effort of management' behind the Louvre show and the museum founding both rest on the single Memoria Chilena portal, and the tent project is a documented failure.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_vp_mc_comp, src_vp_mc_industria, src_vp_mc_bio | 1953-1958 | national library] The portal says she recovered rural song and presented it to a mass public through her own radio programme, records and television, and founded a folk-art museum; its biography calls her compositions and collections a reference point for later Chilean music. The documented actions are consistent with an aim to bring folk culture to a wide audience, but her stated motives are not quoted, so the row is an inference from the actions.

experimentation.rationale: [src_vp_mc_comp, src_vp_mc_art, src_vp_selvedge | 1950s-1964 | national library + magazine] Memoria Chilena records her experimentation with melodies and harmonies and instrumental technique, and the sources describe her trying clay, wire and arpillera work after earlier media and showing it in the Louvre exhibition. The 'experimentation' reading rests on the portal's evaluative sentence and the breadth of media, not on a documented iterative process.

adaptability.rationale: [src_vp_mc_espacios, src_vp_mc_industria, src_vp_eb | 1930s-1966 | national library + encyclopedia] She moved from trains, circuses and restaurants to radio, records, television and European stages, changing repertoire from popular genres to folk song; Britannica records the stay in Paris and the travels in the Soviet Union and Europe. The sequence is documented but the sources give little on how she responded to setbacks, so this is an inference from career movement.

portrait.reason: No rights-clear portrait was found after one bounded retry (about 12 checks). The Wikidata image 'Parra01f.PNG' is a 1973 scan from the Argentine magazine Panorama (author named only as the magazine, tagged low quality, permission note 'published in NYC', PD claimed under Argentine photograph rules and a 1996 rule): a jurisdiction-only claim with no named photographer or item-level statement, 290 x 374 pixels. The Commons 1958 and 1959 album back-cover photographs have unknown photographers and a Chile public-domain tag only (jurisdiction-only). The 1962 Helsinki photograph by Yrjo Lintunen (The People's Archives, Finland) is tagged public domain as a Finnish photograph more than 50 years old, but under the Finnish term of the time it was still protected in 1996, so US copyright was restored; it is rejected. Memoria Chilena portraits are newspaper and book scans whose own site says the digital objects are excluded from its Creative Commons licence. 'Violeta Parra.jpg' is a Flickr photograph of street art, a derivative of someone else's artwork. Next step: obtain a photograph with a named photographer and an explicit licence, for example a request to the Finnish People's Archives or the Violeta Parra Museum / Fundacion Violeta Parra, or a CC photograph of her actual lifetime sitting from a named photographer.
